questions.prompt: Which statement correctly identifies the three areas AI governance is organized around, and matches the course's working definition of AI governance from Lesson 1?
options: The data going in, the model itself, and the decisions/outputs coming out — the same decision-rights-and-accountability idea from data governance, extended to models that act automatically at scale
A separate department from data governance that focuses only on an AI ethics specialist's sign-off before launch
A one-time checklist completed before a model's launch, with no further review needed afterward
The four risk categories — bias, privacy, security, and hallucination — and nothing else
Only the model's technical validation, since the data feeding it is already covered by existing data governance
Compliance with the EU AI Act's risk tiers, since that is the primary binding requirement for any AI system
questions.explain: AI governance is the system of decision rights, accountability, and controls over how an organization sources data for AI, builds and validates models, and takes responsibility for the decisions those models make in production — the same core idea as data governance, extended to a new kind of asset that acts continuously and at scale. It is explicitly not a one-time checklist, not a single ethics hire's job, and not confined to one regulation.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D names real risk categories from Lesson 3, but those are the risks AI governance's controls defend against, not the three organizing areas (data in, the model itself, decisions out) this course is structured around. The two lists are related but are not the same thing — mixing them up is exactly the kind of confusion this question is checking for.

questions.prompt: Match each AI governance role from Lesson 4 to what it's actually accountable for.
right: The cross-functional group that approves new AI use cases, sets policy, and reviews incidents
The business-side person accountable for a specific model's behavior and outcomes in production
The data scientist or ML engineer who develops and trains the model
A reviewer separate from the build team who checks a model for the four risk categories before it's trusted with decisions
questions.explain: The model owner is the business-side person accountable for a model's outcomes in production, not necessarily the person who built it. The model builder is the technical role that develops and trains the model. The independent validator is separate from the build team specifically because the people closest to building something are the least likely to catch their own blind spots. The AI governance council is the cross-functional group that approves use cases and sets policy.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the four AI risk categories from Lesson 3.
options: Bias usually comes from the training data reflecting a real-world imbalance, not from one single bad decision
Privacy risk requires a traditional data breach to occur — a model's own outputs can't expose personal information on their own
Hallucination is specific to generative AI: fluent, confident output that is nonetheless factually wrong
A model can be statistically accurate overall and still be biased against a specific subgroup
Security risk for AI is identical to traditional IT security risk, with no attack types unique to models
questions.explain: Bias typically comes from the data reflecting a real-world imbalance that the model faithfully reproduces at scale, not from a single decision. Hallucination is specific to generative AI producing fluent but factually wrong output. A model's overall accuracy can hide poor performance for a specific subgroup. Privacy risk does not require a traditional breach — the model itself, through memorized training data or outputs that combine information, can become the exposure. Security risk for AI includes attack types traditional IT security doesn't cover, like adversarial inputs, prompt injection, and data poisoning.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Lesson 2 names three consequences of a model's logic being learned rather than authored — scale, inherited risk, and ________, the difficulty of fully explaining why a model produced a specific output.
questions.explain: Opacity follows directly from the logic being statistical and embedded in parameters rather than written as readable rules — it's genuinely harder to predict in advance when a model will behave badly, or to explain after the fact exactly why it made a particular call.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 5, which pairing correctly separates what carries forward unchanged from existing data governance versus what AI governance adds on top?
options: Unchanged: the six data-quality dimensions and existing owner/steward roles. Added: governing the model as a continuously-acting asset, training-specific provenance and consent, and production behavior monitoring.
Unchanged: production behavior monitoring. Added: the six data-quality dimensions, since those didn't exist before AI.
Unchanged: nothing — AI governance replaces data governance's roles and policies entirely rather than extending them.
Unchanged: model versioning. Added: data owners and stewards, since AI introduces the concept of data ownership for the first time.
questions.explain: Lesson 5 is explicit that roles, policies/standards, and the six quality dimensions carry forward unchanged from Data Governance Foundations and Data Quality Management. What AI adds on top is governing the model itself as a new, continuously-acting asset, training-specific provenance/consent concerns, and ongoing production monitoring — none of which has a direct equivalent in plain data governance.

questions.prompt: A report built on bad data gets corrected once someone catches the mistake and rebuilds it. Per Lesson 6, why is a model trained on bad data a different, harder problem?
options: The bad data's patterns get compressed into the model's parameters rather than sitting in a queryable table, so fixing it usually means retraining from scratch rather than editing a row
Models automatically re-validate their own training data every time they make a prediction, so the problem corrects itself over time
A model only consults its training data once, at the exact moment of each individual prediction, so the fix is just as fast as correcting a report
Training data is stored in a separate, easily editable database specifically so bad rows can be deleted after training finishes
questions.explain: Once training finishes, the specific data points a model learned from aren't sitting in a queryable table anymore — they're compressed into statistical patterns distributed across the model's parameters. That makes it much harder to later remove the influence of one bad data point; you usually have to retrain from scratch rather than delete a row, which is exactly why training data decisions get reviewed before training, not just audited after.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 7, ________ asks whether the people whose data is being used actually agreed to this specific use — a separate question from whether that use happens to be legal.
questions.explain: Consent is distinct from legality: a company's terms of service might technically permit a use, but the people described in the data may never have anticipated or agreed to that specific use, especially when it involves training a model that makes decisions about other people.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about how the data-quality dimensions behave differently in training data, per Lesson 8.
options: A mislabeled training example doesn't just contain one wrong fact — it actively teaches the model the wrong association as if it were a real pattern
Duplicate records in training data only waste storage space and have no effect on what pattern the model learns
Missing representation of an entire population segment is a more serious completeness failure than a few missing fields
A model trained on stale data gives a clear visual cue, like a report's date stamp, that its internal picture of 'normal' may be out of date
Data leakage happens when the same or related records appear in both the training data and the data later used to test the model
questions.explain: A mislabeled example actively teaches a wrong association, not just one isolated error. Missing an entire population segment is a more serious completeness failure than scattered missing fields, since it connects directly to bias. Data leakage is exactly duplicate or related records appearing in both training and test data, making test results look better than they really are. Duplicates don't just waste storage — they quietly overweight the pattern they represent. And unlike a dated report, a model gives no visual cue that its internal picture of 'normal' is stale.

questions.prompt: Match each way bias enters through data, per Lesson 9, to its actual description.
right: A proxy variable used to measure something doesn't mean the same thing for every group it's applied to
Training data accurately reflects past decisions that were themselves unequal
Human labelers' own inconsistent judgments become part of the 'ground truth' the model learns to reproduce
The population represented in the training data doesn't match the population the model is actually used on
questions.explain: Historical bias is training data accurately reflecting unequal past decisions. Sampling bias is a mismatch between the training population and the population the model is used on. Measurement bias is a proxy variable that doesn't mean the same thing for everyone it's applied to. Label bias is a labeler's own inconsistency or judgment becoming part of what the model treats as objective truth.

questions.prompt: Two labelers often disagree about whether a transaction is 'fraudulent.' Per Lesson 10, what does that low inter-rater agreement actually signal?
options: That the labeling task itself may be ambiguous, or that the instructions given to labelers weren't clear enough — worth investigating before trusting the labels
That the dataset is too large and should be reduced in size before labeling continues
Nothing of consequence — inter-rater agreement is tracked only for paperwork and has no bearing on label quality
That the model, once trained, will automatically average out the disagreement and produce an unbiased result
questions.explain: Low inter-rater agreement is a signal that the labeling task is ambiguous or that labeler instructions weren't clear enough — either way it's worth investigating before trusting the labels, since whichever judgment gets recorded becomes, as far as the model is concerned, the objective truth for that example.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 11, synthetic data still needs provenance, a bias check against the data it was modeled on, and the same quality bar as real data — plus one disclosure real data doesn't require: a clear, documented statement that it's ________ in the first place.
questions.explain: The one genuinely new governance requirement synthetic data raises is documentation honesty — recording clearly that training experience was synthetic rather than blending it invisibly into 'the training data,' since synthetic and real data carry different kinds of risk that a model card or governance review needs to distinguish.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 12, which section of a model card is specifically described as the one that most often prevents a governance incident, rather than just documenting one after the fact?
options: Out-of-scope use — the section that stops a model validated for one purpose from quietly getting reused for another
Owner and review date — because it is the only section regulators ever actually read
Training data — because listing a model's data sources automatically fixes any bias present in them
Evaluation metrics — because a high aggregate score guarantees the model is safe for any use case
questions.explain: The out-of-scope-use section is the one line that explicitly says what a model was never validated for, which is exactly what prevents a model built for one purpose — say, marketing segmentation — from drifting into a use case, like credit decisions, that nobody ever validated it against.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of a model approval workflow, per Lesson 16, in the order a model version typically passes through them.
items: Development — the model is trained and evaluated against a validation set, and the model card gets drafted
Technical validation — a reviewer other than the builder checks the evaluation methodology itself
Risk/compliance review — a risk or compliance function checks the model against policy for regulated data and risk tier
Business sign-off — the function that owns the decision confirms the model actually solves the business need
Production approval — the final gate that promotes a version's alias to the one serving live traffic
questions.explain: Development produces the trained model and its draft model card. Technical validation checks the evaluation methodology independently of the builder. Risk/compliance review checks the model against policy. Business sign-off confirms the model solves the real business problem. Production approval is the final gate that promotes the version's alias to live traffic — not every model needs all five gates at full weight, but the order reflects increasing organizational stakes.

questions.prompt: Put these links of an AI lineage chain, per Lesson 14, in the order they actually occur.
items: Raw training data is sourced, and goes through transformations before the model ever sees it
Features are engineered from that data, by specific, documented logic
A training run, with specific code and hyperparameters, produces one particular model version
That model version's downstream decisions and consuming systems are tracked going forward
questions.explain: AI lineage extends table lineage one hop further: from raw data, through engineered features, through the specific training run that produced one model version, out to the downstream decisions and systems that version's outputs feed. Missing any link leaves a model you can't fully explain when someone asks why it reached a specific decision.

questions.prompt: Match each model-inventory term from Lesson 13 to what it actually is.
right: The authoritative list of every model an organization runs, with its owner and risk tier
The system that enforces the inventory by making registration the only supported path to production
A model running in production that was never registered — the AI equivalent of shadow IT
A model's record capturing owner, risk tier, version history, status, and a link to its documentation
questions.explain: A model inventory is the list of every model and who owns it. A model registry is the system that enforces the inventory by making registration the only path to production. A shadow model is one running in production that was never registered. A registry entry captures owner, risk tier, version history, status, and a link to the model card.

questions.code:
model: fraud-detector
version: 2.4.0
  MAJOR (2): retrained on expanded feature set — input schema changed
questions.prompt: A fraud-detection model is retrained on an expanded feature set that changes its input schema, as shown above. Per Lesson 15's semantic-versioning convention, what kind of version change is this, and why?
options: A breaking change — a materially different feature set or input schema means downstream consumers may need to adjust
A patch — retraining never changes a model's behavior in a way that matters
A meaningful but non-breaking change — the input schema change doesn't actually affect anything downstream
Not a new version at all — only bug fixes count as a new version under this convention
questions.explain: Lesson 15 classifies a retrain on a materially different dataset, a new feature set, or a different input schema as a breaking change, since downstream consumers may need to adjust. A patch is a low-risk fix like a preprocessing bug fix that doesn't change predictions, and a meaningful non-breaking change keeps the same schema while shifting behavior — neither fits an input-schema change.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 17, what makes loading a malicious model file saved in this format a direct security risk, not just a potential source of bad predictions?
options: pickle deserializes by executing arbitrary code, so a malicious .pkl file can run anything on the machine that loads it
pickle files are always larger than safetensors files, which only slows down inference speed
pickle requires a live internet connection to load, exposing the file to network interception
pickle only works on specific hardware, so a malicious file would simply fail to load rather than execute
questions.explain: Python's pickle format deserializes by executing arbitrary code — a malicious .pkl file can run anything on the machine that loads it, not just produce a bad prediction. That real, long-documented issue is exactly why the industry adopted safetensors, a format designed so loading a model only reads declared tensor data and never executes code.

questions.prompt: Match each AI access surface from Lesson 18 to what it actually is.
right: What most 'users' of a model actually touch — the live API or service that runs predictions
Reveals how a model works even without the weights themselves, through its metadata and documentation
The raw and feature-engineered data a model learned from, often including sensitive or regulated fields
The trained model file itself, which can be extracted, copied, or reverse-engineered if it leaks
questions.explain: Training data is the raw and engineered data a model learned from. Model weights are the trained file itself, which can leak or be reverse-engineered. A registry entry reveals how a model works through its metadata even without the weights. An inference endpoint is the live API most actual users touch. Treating these four as one access point leads to either over-granting or under-granting, which isn't governance — it's just not thinking about it.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about prompt and output governance for generative AI, per Lesson 19.
options: Prompt injection is content or input designed to override a system's intended instructions
Hallucination in a generative model is easy for an automated dashboard metric to catch, the same way a fraud model's score drift is
A user can be the source of a prompt injection attempt, but so can content the model reads, like a document it's summarizing
Human review sampling plays a bigger role for generative systems than for a typical classifier, because free text can be wrong in ways a dashboard metric won't catch
There is a single universal standard format for prompt-and-output governance policies that every vendor already follows
questions.explain: Prompt injection is input, direct or embedded in content the model reads, designed to override intended behavior. A generative model's free-text output can be wrong confidently and fluently in a way a performance dashboard won't flag, which is exactly why human review sampling matters more here than for a classifier whose output is just a score. Lesson 19 is explicit that there's no single standard policy format yet — the practice is still maturing across the industry.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 20, most teams monitor a production model's traffic volume and its latency/error rate well. Which two of the four signal categories does the lesson say are specific to governing a model and most often skipped?
options: Output distribution and business outcome
Volume and latency/errors
Error rate and alert threshold
On-call escalation and model card review
questions.explain: Volume and latency/errors are standard application metrics most teams already watch well. Output distribution (has the shape of predictions shifted?) and business outcome (did the decision track the real-world result?) are specific to governing a model's actual behavior, and are the ones most often skipped.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 21, ________ is a commonly used statistical measure that compares a feature's distribution between a baseline period and a current period to quantify data drift, with practitioners commonly treating a value above 0.2 as a significant shift worth retraining or reviewing.
questions.explain: PSI (Population Stability Index) compares a baseline and current distribution and produces a single number summarizing how much it has shifted. It's widely used because it's simple to compute and easy to explain to a non-technical reviewer, though it isn't the only drift technique — tests like Kolmogorov-Smirnov serve similar purposes.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the AI incident response sequence, per Lesson 22, in order.
items: Detect — a monitoring alert, a user report, or a routine review surfaces the issue
Contain — stop the immediate harm, often by pulling the model out of production or rolling back its alias
Assess impact via lineage — determine which decisions, time period, and downstream systems were actually affected
Notify — tell the affected business owners and anyone required by a regulatory threshold
Remediate — fix the underlying cause, not just the symptom that was noticed
questions.explain: An AI incident is detected, then contained to stop immediate harm (often via alias rollback), then its impact is assessed using the lineage chain, then the right people are notified, and finally the underlying cause is remediated — not just the symptom. This mirrors standard security incident response with AI-specific steps at each stage.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes the three AI governance frameworks named in Lesson 25?
options: The NIST AI RMF is voluntary guidance organized around Govern/Map/Measure/Manage; ISO/IEC 42001 is a certifiable standard for an organization's AI management system; the EU AI Act is binding law that risk-tiers AI systems
The NIST AI RMF is binding law; ISO/IEC 42001 is voluntary guidance; the EU AI Act is a certifiable management-system standard
All three are voluntary frameworks with no certification or legal enforcement mechanism of any kind
ISO/IEC 42001 is binding law in the United States, while the NIST AI RMF applies only within the European Union
The EU AI Act is voluntary guidance that organizations may choose to certify against, the same way they certify against ISO/IEC 42001
The NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001 are both binding law, while the EU AI Act is voluntary industry guidance
questions.explain: The NIST AI RMF is a voluntary U.S. framework giving organizations shared vocabulary and structure (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage). ISO/IEC 42001 is an international standard specifying what an organization's AI management system should look like, built so an organization can seek certification against it. The EU AI Act is binding law that classifies AI systems into risk tiers with different compliance obligations.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B simply swaps which framework is which: it's the NIST AI RMF that's voluntary guidance and the EU AI Act that's binding law, not the reverse. Confusing which one actually carries legal enforcement versus which is a chosen-to-follow standard is exactly the mix-up Lesson 25 is structured to prevent.

questions.prompt: Match each responsible AI principle from Lesson 23 to the governance control the course says actually enforces it.
right: Enforced through the governance roles defined for models, like a named model owner
Delivered through model documentation and model cards
Is the actual mechanism behind every approval workflow, where a human signs off before deployment
Enforced through the bias controls applied to training data
questions.explain: Fairness is enforced through the bias controls on training data from Chapter 2. Transparency is delivered through model documentation and model cards from Chapter 3. Accountability runs through the governance roles — a named model owner — defined in Lesson 4. Human oversight is the actual mechanism behind every approval workflow in Lesson 16, not a separate add-on.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about AI risk management, per Lesson 24.
options: Risk to people affected by the system includes someone being wrongly denied a loan by a model that nobody caught being wrong
A system that's fine for the organization's balance sheet but harmful to the people it touches is not actually a governance failure
Risk to the model itself includes performance degrading as the world changes, or being wrong more often than its stated accuracy suggests
The likelihood-times-impact approach assigns every AI system the same risk tier regardless of context, to keep scoring simple
A system scoring high on both likelihood and impact should receive the most expensive controls, like human review and mandatory approval gates
questions.explain: Risk to people is a real category — someone wrongly denied a loan counts, even if the organization's balance sheet is unaffected. Lesson 24 explicitly says a system that's fine for the organization but harmful to the people it touches is still a governance failure. Risk to the model itself covers drift and understated error rates. Likelihood times impact scores each system individually, and a system high on both gets the most expensive controls, not the same treatment as every other system.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 26, a ________ is a government-imposed requirement with real enforcement mechanisms behind it, as opposed to a framework an organization merely chooses to follow.
questions.explain: A regulation is something a government body requires, with real enforcement mechanisms — distinct from a voluntary framework like the NIST AI RMF, which an organization chooses to follow because it's useful. Lesson 25 and Lesson 26 cover the two frameworks and one binding law side by side specifically to make this distinction visible.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 27, if a high-risk AI system is missing a documented risk-tier justification during an audit, what does that absence actually represent?
options: A finding in itself — the audit's job is to surface the gap, not assume good intent fills it in
Nothing of concern, since risk tiers only need to be assigned once and never revisited
Proof the system is definitely biased, even without any other supporting evidence
A problem only an external regulator, never an internal audit, is allowed to flag
questions.explain: If governance is real, it leaves a paper trail. A missing risk-tier justification for a high-risk system is itself a finding — the audit's job is to surface that gap, not to assume good intent fills it in. Internal audits are specifically meant to catch exactly this kind of gap before an external party does.

questions.prompt: In the Harrow Peak Financial case study (Lesson 28), what specific problem did checking data provenance and applying Lesson 9's bias-in-data training uncover in the five years of historical loan data?
options: One branch's loan officers had informally applied stricter scrutiny to applicants from a particular zip code cluster, baking human bias directly into the 'ground truth' labels
The training data had been accidentally deleted and had to be fully recreated from scratch
The model's code contained a syntax error that prevented it from ever running
Applicants' Social Security numbers were stored in plain text within the training data
questions.explain: The team discovered that for a two-year period, one branch's loan officers had informally applied stricter scrutiny to applicants from a particular zip code cluster — a human bias baked directly into the historical outcome labels the model would otherwise have learned as objective fact. Lesson 9's point that label bias comes from human judgment, not just the algorithm, is exactly what let the team catch it before training.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Brightfield Outfitters case study (Lesson 29) and how it differs from Harrow Peak's (Lesson 28).
options: Brightfield's chatbot produces open-ended language that can't be fully enumerated in advance, unlike Harrow Peak's fixed approve/decline/refer outputs
Because Brightfield's chatbot was risk-tiered lower than Harrow Peak's credit model, Lesson 29 says it required no active monitoring after launch
Governance for Brightfield's chatbot focuses on boundaries — what it must never do — and fast correction, rather than pre-certifying every possible response
The chatbot's known limitation, that it can give fluent but factually wrong answers about specific order details, was documented in its model card before launch
The social-media incident in the case study was resolved without ever being logged in the model's own record
questions.explain: Brightfield's chatbot produces open-ended text that can't be exhaustively tested the way Harrow Peak's three fixed outputs could, so its governance strategy focuses on boundaries and fast correction instead. Its known limitation about order-detail accuracy was written into its model card before launch. Despite being risk-tiered lower than the credit model, the lesson says it was still tiered high enough to require active monitoring, not a launch-and-forget posture — and the social-media incident was logged in the model's record, not minimized.

questions.prompt: Put these first steps of building an AI governance program, per Lesson 30, in the order the course says to build them.
items: Step 1 — Name a single, specific accountable owner for AI governance overall and for each individual AI system
Step 2 — Inventory every AI system actually in use, including any shadow AI nobody approved
Step 3 — Risk-tier everything in the inventory using a likelihood-times-impact method
Step 4 — Set training-data standards (provenance, quality, bias checks) starting with the highest-risk systems first
Step 5 — Require model-card documentation for anything above the lowest risk tier
questions.explain: Lesson 30 is explicit that order matters more than most people expect: naming an accountable owner and building a real inventory (Steps 1-2) come first because every later step depends on both existing already. Risk-tiering (Step 3) then decides how much effort later steps deserve, training-data standards (Step 4) apply that tiering to the highest-risk systems first, and documentation (Step 5) is required above the lowest tier — most organizations that fail at AI governance tried to start with model cards or audits before anyone had agreed who owned what.
